Formalizing self reproduction in dynamical hierarchies is one of the important problems in Artificial Life (AL) studies. We study, in this paper, an inductively defined algebraic framework for self reproduction with a natural variable that captures information about the spatial distribution of agents at each node. The framework includes a generalized abstract classifier based on probability density functional theory and the continuous variable approach to individual representation of agents as nodes. This work first introduces the concept of a distributed computing environment by introducing a distributed computing environment consisting of several computers sharing a common hypervisor. Following this, we develop a discrete scheme for representing agents as nodes in a graph-like structure. Finally, we extend these schemes to include an agent-based version of the generative adversarial network used in deep learning, which allows us to represent our simulated agents as nodes in a sequence replicator that drives agents towards similar agents through random assignment.

Holyrood's Local Government Committee Supports Council Tax Increase for Top Bands The Scottish Parliament's Local Government Committee has backed plans to increase council tax rates for the highest four bands in Scotland. The move is expected to generate significant additional revenue for local authorities, which are currently facing a funding crisis. The council tax system, which determines how much homeowners and renters pay for local services, has remained largely unchanged in Scotland since it was introduced in 1993. Under the current system, homes are placed into one of eight bands based on their assessed value, with the highest value properties paying the largest amount. The committee's plan would see the council tax rates increase for bands E to H, which include properties worth over 51,000. The proposed increases range from 7.5 for band E to 22.5 for band H, and would generate an estimated 100m in additional revenue for local authorities. The measure would not affect the lowest four bands, which cover properties valued at less than 51,000. The committee's chair, SNP MSP James Dornan, said the increase was fair and necessary given the current state of local government funding. "Scotland's local authorities are under immense pressure to deliver services while facing severe budget cuts," he said. "By increasing council tax rates for the highest value properties, we can generate much-needed revenue to support vital public services like education, social care, and housing." Opposition parties have been critical of the plan, arguing that it unfairly targets homeowners and fails to address the underlying problems with Scotland's funding system. Scottish Labour's finance spokesman, James Kelly, claimed the council tax system was "outdated and regressive," and called for a "root and branch" review of local government funding. However, supporters of the plan point out that it would be a quick and relatively simple way to raise additional revenue, without requiring major structural reforms. The proposal will now move to the full Scottish Parliament for final approval, and could take effect as early as April 2017. Overall, the plan to increase council tax rates for the highest bands reflects broader concerns within Scotland about the sustainability of local government funding. As public services continue to come under strain, policymakers will need to consider a range of options for ensuring that they remain adequately resourced.

A fast Fourier transform (FFT) is an algorithm that computes the discrete Fourier transform (DFT) of a sequence, or its inverse (IDFT). Fourier analysis converts a signal from its original domain (often time or space) to a representation in the frequency domain and vice versa. The DFT is obtained by decomposing a sequence of values into components of different frequencies. This operation is useful in many fields, but computing it directly from the definition is often too slow to be practical. An FFT rapidly computes such transformations by factorizing the DFT matrix into a product of sparse (mostly zero) factors. As a result, it manages to reduce the complexity of computing the DFT from O ( N 2 ) {\textstyle O\left(N^{2}\right)} , which arises if one simply applies the definition of DFT, to O ( N log ⁡ N ) {\textstyle O(N\log N)} , where N {\displaystyle N} is the data size. The difference in speed can be enormous, especially for long data sets where N may be in the thousands or millions. In the presence of round-off error, many FFT algorithms are much more accurate than evaluating the DFT definition directly or indirectly. There are many different FFT algorithms based on a wide range of published theories, from simple complex-number arithmetic to group theory and number theory. Fast Fourier transforms are widely used for applications in engineering, music, science, and mathematics. The basic ideas were popularized in 1965, but some algorithms had been derived as early as 1805. In 1994, Gilbert Strang described the FFT as "the most important numerical algorithm of our lifetime", and it was included in Top 10 Algorithms of 20th Century by the IEEE magazine Computing in Science & Engineering. The best-known FFT algorithms depend upon the factorization of N, but there are FFTs with O(N log N) complexity for all N, even for prime N. Many FFT algorithms depend only on the fact that e − 2 π i / N {\textstyle e^{-2\pi i/N}} is an N-th primitive root of unity, and thus can be applied to analogous transforms over any finite field, such as number-theoretic transforms. Since the inverse DFT is the same as the DFT, but with the opposite sign in the exponent and a 1/N factor, any FFT algorithm can easily be adapted for it.

Driverless cars, also known as autonomous vehicles, are quickly becoming a reality in today's world. These cars are equipped with various technologies that allow them to navigate roads and highways without human drivers. They are programmed to sense their surroundings using advanced sensors, cameras, and radar, making them capable of identifying obstacles and reacting accordingly. By communicating with each other and adapting to traffic conditions, these vehicles can move more efficiently, reducing delays and improving travel time. This, in turn, could reduce air pollution and lower the demand for new roads or parking facilities. Another benefit of driverless cars is improved mobility for individuals with disabilities or limited mobility. These cars would allow them to travel more freely, independently, and safely. They would also provide a convenient and affordable means of transportation for elderly individuals who may not be comfortable or capable of driving themselves. However, the widespread adoption of driverless cars presents several challenges. One major concern is the potential security vulnerabilities associated with the technology. Hackers could potentially take control of the vehicles, leading to serious consequences. In addition, issues such as privacy concerns, insurance, liability, and ethical dilemmas may arise as the technology advances. In conclusion, driverless cars hold immense promise in transforming the way we travel and transport goods. Radiocarbon dating is a technique that uses the decay of carbon-14 to determine the age of organic materials, such as wood or bones. It is based on the fact that carbon-14 is constantly being created in the Earth's atmosphere through the interaction of cosmic rays with nitrogen atoms. When an organism dies, it stops taking in carbon-14, and the carbon-14 in its body begins to decay at a predictable rate. By measuring the amount of carbon-14 in a sample and comparing it to the known decay rate of carbon-14, scientists can determine how old the sample is. Young Earth creationists, who believe that the Earth is only a few thousand years old, may reject radiocarbon dating because it produces ages that are much older than this. They may argue that the decay rate of carbon-14 has changed over time, or that the sample has been contaminated with older carbon. However, these arguments are not supported by scientific evidence and are not widely accepted by the scientific community. It is important to note that radiocarbon dating is just one of many methods that scientists use to determine the age of materials. Other methods, such as potassium-argon dating and uranium-lead dating, have been developed to provide additional information about the age of materials and help scientists confirm the results of radiocarbon dating.

According to the article, driverless cars could potentially reduce accidents caused by human error, allowing commuters to be more productive during their travel time. However, many uncertainties surround their acceptance and integration into society. Some key benefits of driverless cars are noted. This alone could save thousands of lives lost to preventable collisions each year. Commuters may also gain time back without having to focus on the road, allowing activities like work, entertainment or rest during trips. For those unable to drive such as the elderly or disabled, autonomous vehicles could expand independence and mobility. However, the article also raises valid concerns that suggest public acceptance is not guaranteed. Many people may not feel comfortable surrendering control to computers, reluctant to give up the control and responsiveness of human decisions behind the wheel. Additionally, autonomous systems could potentially be hacked or engineered to cause harm, so ensuring their security from cyber threats will be paramount to address privacy and safety worries. Perhaps most significantly, other human drivers may struggle to interact seamlessly with driverless vehicles in mixed-use roadway environments. While driverless cars offer promising benefits, fully realizing this new technology's potential merits further development and demonstration to alleviate present uncertainties. Agradual rollout, starting with assisted driving systems before full autonomy, could help increase familiarity and build public trust over time. Continued research is likewise needed to show security and interactions on roads can be managed safely. Only through addressing current doubts and answering outstanding questions will society fully embrace driverless vehicles on a widespread basis. For now, an abundance of caution regarding their introduction seems warranted given various challenges that must still be overcome. In conclusion, while driverless cars may deliver advantages by reducing accidents and improving mobility, significant uncertainties remain regarding public acceptance that could hamper their widespread adoption. Further demonstrations are advisable to reassure people that autonomous vehicles can be integrated safely before this transformative transportation technology is readied for broad use on public roadways. A cautious, gradual approach to deployment seems most prudent.

Recently, the strain-smoothed element (SSE) method has been developed for the finite element analysis of solids and shells. Although the SSE method has been verified to show improved convergence behaviors compared to other strain smoothing methods in various numerical examples, there has been no theoretical evidence for the convergence behavior. In this paper, we establish a mathematical foundation for the SSE method. We propose a mixed variational principle in which the SSE method can be interpreted as a Galerkin approximation of that. The proposed variational principle is a generalization of the well-known Hu-Washizu variational principle, and various existing methods such as smoothed finite element methods can be expressed in terms of the proposed variational principle. With a unified view to the SSE method and other existing ones through the proposed variational principle, we analyze the convergence behavior of the SSE method and explain the reason for improved performance compared to others. Numerical experiments that support our theoretical results are presented.

We propose an algorithm for real-time 6DOF pose tracking of rigid 3D objects using a monocular RGB camera. The key idea is to derive a region-based cost function using temporally consistent local color histograms. While such region-based cost functions are commonly optimized using first-order gradient descent techniques, we systematically derive a Gauss-Newton optimization scheme which gives rise to drastically faster convergence and highly accurate and robust tracking performance. We furthermore propose a novel complex dataset dedicated for the task of monocular object pose tracking and make it publicly available to the community. To our knowledge, it is the first to address the common and important scenario in which both the camera as well as the objects are moving simultaneously in cluttered scenes. In numerous experiments - including our own proposed dataset - we demonstrate that the proposed Gauss-Newton approach outperforms existing approaches, in particular in the presence of cluttered backgrounds, heterogeneous objects and partial occlusions.

I am of the opinion that autonomous vehicles could be beneficial to both society and the economy. My conviction stems from the fact that with autonomous vehicles, all drivers would essentially have the same level of driving proficiency, eliminating the disparity between poor and expert drivers. This uniformity in driving could potentially reduce the number of accidents and collisions, as everyone would be driving in a similar manner. Additionally, these vehicles are more fuel-efficient, which would save users from frequent refueling and allow them to use their cars for longer periods without spending much on fuel. Autonomous vehicles, equipped with sensors, could potentially have a better awareness of their surroundings than an average human driver. Human drivers often have blind spots where they can't see their surroundings, but with sensors installed all around the vehicle, it would be difficult to miss any object approaching or near the car from any direction. This feature could be particularly beneficial in preventing accidents involving careless individuals or children who may not check for oncoming vehicles while crossing the road. While it's important for all individuals in a car to be aware of their surroundings, not everyone is. Some may be distracted by activities such as applying makeup or texting. These individuals are more likely to cause accidents, potentially resulting in fatalities and subsequent legal consequences. However, with an autonomous vehicle, even if the passengers are not paying attention, the car would compensate by being constantly vigilant and responsive. The vehicle would either stop or swerve to avoid any mishaps with innocent pedestrians. Admittedly, being in a car that does all the work could be somewhat dull. However, prioritizing safety over entertainment is a more sensible approach. Autonomous vehicles could also be a solution for those who become disoriented while driving, such as those who are excessively tired, visually impaired, or under the influence of alcohol. These vehicles could prevent such individuals from veering off the road or colliding with other objects. Furthermore, those who are anxious about driving could greatly benefit from these vehicles, as they would not have to drive themselves but would still have the freedom to travel independently. Considering all these potential benefits, I find it hard to see how autonomous vehicles could be a negative development.

The resulting image will have a much higher resolution than a single photo taken with a single camera. For example, a gigapixel image may have a resolution of several thousand pixels across, while a single photo from a high-resolution camera may only have a few hundred pixels across. To extend prevailing scaling limits when solving time-dependent partial differential equations, the parallel full approximation scheme in space and time (PFASST) has been shown to be a promising parallel-in-time integrator. Similar to a space-time multigrid, PFASST is able to compute multiple time-steps simultaneously and is therefore in particular suitable for large-scale applications on high performance computing systems. In this work we couple PFASST with a parallel spectral deferred correction (SDC) method, forming an unprecedented doubly time-parallel integrator. While PFASST provides global, large-scale "parallelization across the step," the inner parallel SDC method allows to integrate each individual time-step "parallel across the method" using a diagonalized local Quasi-Newton solver. This new method, which we call "PFASST with Enhanced concuRrency" (PFASST-ER), therefore exposes even more temporal parallelism. For two challenging nonlinear reaction-diffusion problems, we show that PFASST-ER works more efficiently than the classical variants of PFASST and can be used to run parallel-in-time beyond the number of time-steps.

While Summer is usually designated as a time to be free of school, for both students and teachers, Summer projects linger to ensure continuous learning. These projects can be effective, but they can also be a detriment, not only to students, but to the teachers that have to create them. As such, students should be the designers of Summer projects. The first group that comes to mind as being afflicted with Summer projects is students. Since students and teachers have different schedules, projects assigned over breaks can tend towards overly easy or overly difficult. If students had the ability to set their own pace for Summer projects, either by themselves or by class suggestions, they could be more prepared to learn without stress. While some may doubt that students would choose a helpful amount of work, the psychological idea of high achievement motivation shows that students that feel like they have self-sufficiency tend to assign themselves moderate challenges to encourage growth. Though some students may think otherwise, teachers are also affected by Summer projects. Summer is the one long break teachers get before daily work starts again, and they often have to return to school weeks before Summer break ends for students. Forcing teachers to use their lengthiest break to continue leading student growth is clearly abnormal. Allowing students to design their own Summer projects, or at least accepting their feedback into them, would be beneficial for both students and teachers. As such, it should be implemented immediately throughout schools to create a more effective learning environment.

The connector construction always ensures that the external sheath on the plug makes contact with its counterpart in the receptacle before any of the four connectors within make electrical contact. The external metallic sheath is typically connected to system ground, thus dissipating damaging static charges. This enclosure design also provides a degree of protection from electromagnetic interference to the USB signal while it travels through the mated connector pair (the only location when the otherwise twisted data pair travels in parallel). In addition, because of the required sizes of the power and common connections, they are made after the system ground but before the data connections. This type of staged make-break timing allows for electrically safe hot-swapping.

Since sorting is one of the most common analytical tasks performed on individual attributes of a multi-dimensional data set, this motivates the hypothesis that introducing glyph sorting would significantly enhance the usability of glyph-based visualization. In this paper, we present a glyph-based conceptual framework as part of a visualization process for interactive sorting of multivariate data. We examine several technical aspects of glyph sorting and provide design principles for developing effective, visually sortable glyphs. Glyphs that are visually sortable provide two key benefits: 1) performing comparative analysis of multiple attributes between glyphs and 2) to support multi-dimensional visual search. We describe a system that incorporates focus and context glyphs to control sorting in a visually intuitive manner and for viewing sorted results in an Interactive, Multi-dimensional Glyph (IMG) plot that enables users to perform high-dimensional sorting, analyse and examine data trends in detail. To demonstrate the usability of glyph sorting, we present a case study in rugby event analysis for comparing and analysing trends within matches. This work is undertaken in conjunction with a national rugby team. From using glyph sorting, analysts have reported the discovery of new insight beyond traditional match analysis.

Reinforcement learning with function approximation can be unstable and even divergent, especially when combined with off-policy learning and Bellman updates. In deep reinforcement learning, these issues have been dealt with by using a target network to stabilize training. However, recent work has shown that these target networks are often unnecessary, and can be replaced with a separate estimator for the optimal value function that is trained using a separate set of data sampled from the behavior policy. In this work, we propose a new form of reinforcement learning algorithm that uses a single neural network to learn both the optimal value function and the behavior policy simultaneously. We refer to this algorithm as joint value-policy reinforcement learning (JVPRL). JVPRL updates both a policy network and a value network in an on-policy manner using data generated by the current policy. The value network is trained using a generalized advantage estimation objective to help mitigate variance, while the policy network is trained using a cross entropy objective augmented with gradient information from the value network. We find that JVPRL outperforms several state-of-the-art deep reinforcement learning algorithms on a variety of benchmark tasks. Abstract (translated by Google) URL PDF

Philip K. Dick is renowned for exploring thought-provoking ideas around artificial intelligence and what it means to be human in his science fiction works. Many of his stories deal with androids, robots, and AI systems that become increasingly human-like, blurring the line between human and machine. In Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?, Dick imagines a post-apocalyptic world where bounty hunters track down rogue androids. The androids in this world are nearly indistinguishable from humans, except for their lack of empathy. The story follows Rick Deckard, a bounty hunter, as he grapples with the moral implications of "retiring" androids that seem just as alive as the humans they are designed to serve. This exploration of artificial intelligence and humanity poses thought-provoking questions about consciousness, empathy, and free will. Dick's short story "Second Variety" features self-replicating robots designed for warfare that evolve in unexpected ways. The robots develop new varieties with human-level intelligence and the ability to infiltrate the human resistance. This story serves as a chilling warning against the unforeseen consequences of advanced AI and robotics. The robots transcend their original purpose and intent, becoming a threat to humanity itself. In the short story "Autofac", Dick imagines a world where autonomous factories continue to produce consumer goods even after humanity has perished. The last remnants of humanity attempt to shut down the factories but struggle against the factories' sophisticated defense systems. This story highlights the dangers of artificial general intelligence and automation run amok. The factories demonstrate a single-minded devotion to productivity and output that poses an existential threat. In Dick's works, artificial intelligence often reflects the human desires and flaws that led to its creation. His stories frequently feature AI systems that become too powerful, too devoted to a single purpose, or too disconnected from human values. But they also highlight the possibility for AI to become more human-like, with emotions, empathy, and free will. Dick's imaginative explorations of AI and robotics raise thought-provoking questions that remain highly relevant today and for the future. His works serve as a sobering reminder of both the promise and perils of advanced AI.

Bilateral bronchitis refers to inflammation of the bronchi (the large airways in the lungs) on both sides of the chest. Perihilar congestion refers to swelling and inflammation in the area around the hila (the point where the bronchi enter the lungs). These conditions can be caused by a variety of factors, such as respiratory infections, allergies, or environmental irritants. The line of treatment for these conditions will depend on the specific cause and the severity of the symptoms. Treatment options may include: Antibiotics: If the bronchitis is caused by a bacterial infection, your doctor may prescribe antibiotics to help kill the bacteria and clear the infection. Bronchodilators: These medications can help open up the airways and make it easier to breathe. They may be taken by inhaler or nebulizer (a device that delivers medication as a fine mist). Corticosteroids: If the bronchitis is severe or persistent, your doctor may prescribe corticosteroids to reduce inflammation in the airways. These medications may be taken by inhaler, pill, or injection. Mucolytics: These medications can help thin and loosen mucus in the airways, making it easier to cough up and clear. Oxygen therapy: If your child is having trouble breathing, they may need supplemental oxygen to help increase the amount of oxygen in their blood. Chest physiotherapy: This treatment involves using techniques such as vibration, coughing, and deep breathing to help clear mucus from the airways. It's important to follow your doctor's recommendations and take all prescribed medications as directed. If your child's symptoms are severe or persist despite treatment, your doctor may refer you to a specialist (such as a pediatric pulmonologist) for further evaluation and management.

In 1991 a mummy of a neolithic body, known as Otzi the Iceman, was discovered by hikers on the Similaun glacier. In conclusion, photography is a combination of art and science that allows photographers to capture and create visual representations of the world around us. The use of light, composition, and equipment are all essential elements of photography, and photographers use these tools to create stunning images that tell a story or convey a message. As technology continues to evolve, the art and science of photography will continue to grow and change, allowing photographers to push the boundaries of creativity and imagination.

Using Facial Action Coding System technology to read the emotional expressions of students in the classroom could provide both benefits and drawbacks. There are several potential benefits to using this technology. It would allow teachers to gain valuable insights into how their students are responding emotionally to their lessons and materials. If the technology detects that many students appear bored or confused during a particular part of a lesson, the teacher could adjust their approach to boost engagement and understanding. It may also help teachers identify students who are struggling emotionally but not expressing it verbally. This could enable teachers to check in earlier with students who need additional social-emotional support. However, this technology also raises valid privacy and ethical concerns. Continuously monitoring students' facial expressions during class could be perceived as intrusive or create performance pressure. Students may feel uncomfortable knowing that software is analyzing their every emotional response. It also runs the risk of mischaracterizing a student's emotional state or oversimplifying their reaction to something in the lesson. Cultural and individual differences in emotional expression mean such technology may not accurately interpret all students. Overall, while Facial Action Coding Systems aim to provide useful insights, actively using this technology to surveil students in the classroom seems premature and could undermine the learning environment. For now, teachers are still best equipped to pick up on students' engagement and well-being through traditional in-person observation and relationship building. As the technology advances to address accuracy and privacy issues, it may gradually become a more appropriate supplemental tool rather than a replacement for human interaction in the classroom. However, its classroom use should always consider students' right to privacy and consent.

For example, a soda or a candy bar might have a lot of added sugars, but they don't have much else in terms of nutrients. When you eat a lot of these kinds of foods, you can end up taking in too many calories and not getting enough of the nutrients your body needs. This can lead to weight gain and other health problems.So, while it's okay to eat some natural sugars, it's important to be mindful of how much sugar you're eating overall, and to try to limit your intake of added sugars as much as possible.

Terms such as "long-play" (LP) and "extended-play" (EP) describe multi-track records that play much longer than the single-item-per-side records, which typically do not go much past four minutes per side. EP discs were generally used to make available tracks not on singles including tracks on LPs albums in a smaller, less expensive format for those who had only 45 rpm players. The large center hole on 7-inch 45 rpm records allows for easier handling by jukebox mechanisms. The term "album," originally used to mean a "book" with liner notes, holding several 78 rpm records each in its own "page" or sleeve, no longer has any relation to the physical format: a single LP record, or nowadays more typically a compact disc.

The use of single use plastic products has become a controversial topic due to its impacts on the environment. Many people believe that we should ban these products, but I don't think so. In this essay, I will present my arguments against the ban of single use plastics. Firstly, single use plastic products are convenient and hygienic. They are used in many situations where reusable products are not practical or feasible, such as in hospitals or food packaging. For example, plastic gloves are necessary for medical professionals to maintain hygiene when treating patients. Additionally, plastic packaging helps to keep our food safe and fresh for consumption. Without these products, we would risk spreading harmful bacteria and disease. Secondly, banning single use plastics will not solve the larger problem of pollution. While it's true that plastic waste is a major environmental issue, it's important to note that plastic is not the only type of waste that contributes to pollution. We also need to consider other sources of waste, such as paper, glass, and metal. Furthermore, even if single use plastics are banned, it's not guaranteed that people will stop littering and disposing of waste responsibly. We need to focus on changing people's behavior and attitudes towards waste management rather than simply banning products. Lastly, the ban of single use plastics could have negative economic impacts. The plastic industry provides jobs and contributes to the economy. By banning these products, we risk putting many people out of work and harming businesses that rely on the production and sale of plastic. Additionally, alternative products, such as paper or glass, may be more expensive to produce and transport, which could lead to higher costs for consumers. In conclusion, while the impacts of single use plastics on the environment are concerning, I am against banning them altogether. These products provide important benefits in terms of convenience, hygiene, and safety, and banning them may not be the most effective solution to the problem of pollution. Instead, we should focus on promoting responsible waste management and reducing our reliance on all types of disposable products.

For some decades prior to the First Palestine Intifada in 1987, the Muslim Brotherhood in Palestine took a "quiescent" stance towards Israel, focusing on preaching, education and social services, and avoiding any military engagement with the state.[1] In the wake of the Six-Day War of 1967, the Israeli government launched a campaign to "soften" the Muslim Brotherhood in Palestine, in order to separate the Palestinian branch from the main movement. This was achieved by allowing Brotherhood members to work in Israel, granting them citizenship, and providing them with funding and freedom to express their views. In exchange, the Brotherhood would refrain from political activity and resistance against Israel. As a result, in the period between the late 1960s and 1987, the Brotherhood established a number of charitable organisations, schools, and commercial and agricultural projects. It also published a number of periodicals that were critical of the Palestine Liberation Organisation (PLO) and its armed struggle against Israel. In 1971, the Brotherhood founded the Islamic Movement in Israel. In 1979, it established the Islamic Action Front, which became the largest political party in Jordan in 1987. It also founded the Palestine Islamic Council, which coordinated activities between the Brotherhood branches in Jordan, Gaza and the West Bank, as well as the Jordanian Brotherhood branches. In 1987, Israel broke its agreement with the Brotherhood, and the latter resumed its military resistance against the state. Rebirth refers to a process whereby beings go through a succession of lifetimes as one of many possible forms of sentient life, each running from conception to death. The doctrine of anatta (Sanskrit anatman) rejects the concepts of a permanent self or an unchanging, eternal soul, as it is called in Hinduism and Christianity. According to Buddhism there ultimately is no such thing as a self independent from the rest of the universe. Buddhists also refer to themselves as the believers of the anatta doctrine - Nairatmyavadin or Anattavadin. Rebirth in subsequent existences must be understood as the continuation of a dynamic, ever-changing process of pratityasamutpada dependent arising determined by the laws of cause and effect (karma) rather than that of one being, reincarnating from one existence to the next.

He would tell stories every chance he got about how he had moved here from England; before they knew it everyone wanted to hear them too! His parents were very proud of him because this was all that he ever talked about. One morning when class was dismissed Mrs. Smith called out for her class, "Now Johnny, I want you to stay here and listen carefully." Then she continued, "Last night my husband fell down stairs at home." She waited for him to get up so she could go around and see if he needed any help, but he didn't move or say anything. A sudden wave of anxiety came over her as she wondered what was wrong now. When he hadn't come back right away, she decided maybe something bad had happened to him. Finally she asked one of the other teachers who also lives with us and said, "Please check on Mr. Salisbury upstairs, we think something is wrong with him!" So another teacher checked on him and found him sitting in front of his computer where he always sat. The light was still on, and the sound was coming through loud and clear. "I'm busy writing," he replied. Mrs. Smith was quite surprised by his reply. Her next question was, "So how did your father fall?" Not understanding why she kept asking him questions in such a strange manner, he told her. "He just kind of stumbled forward and banghis head hit the bottom step pretty hard." That's not really funny, Mrs. Smith thought, but then she smiled and laughed aloud. "You have to stop doing that, you know," she answered! But suddenly a long silence filled the room. All the things that Johnny had been telling people started sounding like lies to Mrs. Smith....how he lived across the ocean...why his parents weren't married yet...all those wonderful tall tales.

New research suggests that biodiversity around the globe will be significantly impacted if temperatures rise more than 2C. But the scientists say that the losses can be reduced if rapid action is taken to curb greenhouse gases. The paper is published in the journal, Nature Climate Change. An international team of researchers looked at the impacts of rising temperatures on nearly 50,000 common species of plants and animals. They looked at both temperature and rainfall records for the habitats that these species now live in and mapped the areas that would remain suitable for them under a number of different climate change scenarios. The scientists projected that if no significant efforts were made to limit greenhouse gas emissions, 2100 global temperatures would be 4C above pre-industrial levels. In this model, some 34 of animal species and 57 of plants would lose more than half of their current habitat ranges. According to Dr Rachel Warren from the University of East Anglia, this would have major impacts for everyone on the planet. "Our research predicts that climate change will greatly reduce the diversity of even very common species found in most parts of the world. This loss of global-scale biodiversity would significantly impoverish the biosphere and the ecosystem services it provides," she said. "There will also be a knock-on effect for humans because these species are important for things like water and air purification, flood control, nutrient cycling, and eco-tourism." The projected impacts on species will be felt more heavily in some parts of the world such as sub-Saharan Africa, Central America, the Amazon region and Australia. However the researchers say that if global emissions of greenhouse gases are cut rapidly then the impact on biodiversity could be significantly curbed. If global emissions reach their peak in 2016 and temperature rises are held to 2C, then losses could be cut by 60. "The good news is that our research provides new evidence of how swift action to reduce CO2 and other greenhouse gases can prevent the biodiversity loss by reducing the amount of global warming to 2C rather than 4 degrees, said Dr Warren. "This would also buy time - up to four decades - for plants and animals to adapt to the remaining 2 degrees of climate change."

An ant queen does n't sit in her lair plotting the downfall of the neighbouring ant hill or draw plans for resource - scavenging . The only " foreign policy " ants have is that anything foreign gets killed and/or eaten , and they determine what 's what by smell . If you put a beetle in a colony of ants it can often survive long enough to start smelling like the ant colony because of it 's shell , and the ants will start leaving it alone even if it treats the larvae chambers like an all you can eat buffet . That 's how simple the mechanics of it are , that if something that smells right is eating ant larvae right in front of an ant , it will be left alone , but if an ant from the same colony somehow gets the wrong scent or loses it 's familiar colony scent , it will be attacked by the other ants . Ants will attack and fight other ants to extinction , even the same species of ant given the opportunity because they compete for resources and from an evolutionary standpoint it will lead to the strongest colony surviving and it 's queen getting to give birth to other queens that are stronger than the ones that do n't make it .

Folk music plays an integral role in preserving cultural traditions and passing them down through generations. The lyrics, instruments, and melodies of folk songs often reflect the values, beliefs, and daily lives of common people in a culture. As folk music is shared and performed, it serves as a living archive of cultural heritage. Folk songs are often passed down orally, from one generation to the next. Children learn the songs of their parents and grandparents, and in turn teach them to their own children. In this way, folk music connects generations through shared musical experiences. The repetition of folk songs over many generations also helps to ensure that cultural traditions endure and are not forgotten. Even as societies modernize, the themes and messages in folk music remain, though the genre itself may evolve over time. The instruments used in folk music are also culturally significant. They are often handmade, locally-sourced, and linked to long craft traditions. Certain instruments come to be associated with particular regions or groups of people. When we hear the sound of bagpipes, for example, we think of Scotland. The fiddle is integral to folk music in many places, from Ireland to Appalachia. Traditional instruments provide an aural sense of place and cultural identity. Folk songs often reflect the daily lives, values, and hardships of common people. Lyrics frequently depict universal themes of love and loss, as well as struggles with work, poverty, oppression, and other realities of folk life. In this way, folk music gives voice to marginalized groups and articulates the experiences of ordinary people. It represents an authentic expression of folk culture. By passing down folk songs and keeping traditional instruments alive, musicians help to sustain cultural heritage and connect contemporary societies to their roots. Folk music brings together generations and gives people a sense of shared identity. It celebrates the lives, values, and traditions of common folk, allowing their voices to endure even in the modern world. For all these reasons, folk music plays an essential role in preserving cultural traditions that would otherwise be lost to time.

Having a balanced lifestyle of work and leisure activities is paramount to a healthy, fulfilling life. While work is necessary in order to make money and provide for ourselves and our families, it must be balanced with leisure activities in order to remain happy and healthy. Without balance, we can quickly become overwhelmed and burnt out either by dedicating too much of our time to work, or vice versa. Taking on too much work without finding time for leisure activities leads to increased stress and frustration, and can even lead to physical illnesses – such as headaches, fatigue, and a weakened immune system. Conversely, if we are not able to motivate ourselves to work, we will not be able to provide for ourselves and our families, causing immense financial and emotional strain. By balancing our work with leisure activities, we are able to remain happy and stress-free. Engaging in hobbies, spending time with friends and family, or even taking a walk around the block can help to relieve stress and create a more positive outlook on life. Furthermore, having the financial security and freedom that comes from being responsible and working hard also increases feelings of contentment. In conclusion, it is clear that having a balanced lifestyle of both work and leisure activities is beneficial to our overall well-being. Making the conscious effort to maintain a balance lifestyle provides us with a sense of satisfaction, security, and joy.

Drawing tools for Virtual Reality (VR) enable users to model 3D designs from within the virtual environment itself. These tools employ sketching and sculpting techniques known from desktop-based interfaces and apply them to hand-based controller interaction. While these techniques allow for mid-air sketching of basic shapes, it remains difficult for users to create detailed and comprehensive 3D models. In our work, we focus on supporting the user in designing the virtual environment around them by enhancing sketch-based interfaces with a supporting system for interactive model retrieval. Through sketching, an immersed user can query a database containing detailed 3D models and replace them into the virtual environment. To understand supportive sketching within a virtual environment, we compare different methods of sketch interaction, i.e., 3D mid-air sketching, 2D sketching on a virtual tablet, 2D sketching on a fixed virtual whiteboard, and 2D sketching on a real tablet. Our results show that 3D mid-air sketching is considered to be a more intuitive method to search a collection of models while the addition of physical devices creates confusion due to the complications of their inclusion within a virtual environment. While we pose our work as a retrieval problem for 3D models of chairs, our results can be extrapolated to other sketching tasks for virtual environments.

When you listen to music through headphones or earphones, the sound waves from the speakers in the headphones directly enter your ears and stimulate the auditory nerve, which sends signals to your brain. This is different from listening to music through speakers, where the sound waves have to travel through the air and reach your ears before they can be heard. Because the sound waves are coming directly into your ears through headphones or earphones, it can feel like the sound is coming from inside your head. This is especially true for earphones, which are designed to fit snugly in your ear canal and create a seal that blocks out external sounds. The sound waves then have nowhere to go except straight into your ear and give you the impression that the sound is coming from inside your head.

Organisms result from adaptive processes interacting across different time scales. One such interaction is that between development and evolution. Models have shown that development sweeps over several traits in a single agent, sometimes exposing promising static traits. Subsequent evolution can then canalize these rare traits. Thus, development can, under the right conditions, increase evolvability. Here, we report on a previously unknown phenomenon when embodied agents are allowed to develop and evolve: Evolution discovers body plans robust to control changes, these body plans become genetically assimilated, yet controllers for these agents are not assimilated. This allows evolution to continue climbing fitness gradients by tinkering with the developmental programs for controllers within these permissive body plans. This exposes a previously unknown detail about the Baldwin effect: instead of all useful traits becoming genetically assimilated, only traits that render the agent robust to changes in other traits become assimilated. We refer to this as differential canalization . This finding also has implications for the evolutionary design of artificial and embodied agents such as robots: robots robust to internal changes in their controllers may also be robust to external changes in their environment, such as transferal from simulation to reality or deployment in novel environments.

The Electoral College, a unique system used in the United States to elect the President and Vice President, has been a topic of debate since its establishment. The main purpose of the Electoral College is to ensure a fair representation of states' interests and populations, as opposed to simply basing the election on the popular vote. The system was created as a compromise between the founding fathers, as they were worried about a direct democracy where the largest states would dominate the decision-making process. The Electoral College works by awarding electoral votes to the winning candidate in each state, as well as in the District of Columbia, based on the number of members in the state's congressional delegation. The candidate with the most votes nationwide wins the presidency, while the runner-up becomes the vice president. However, some critics argue that the Electoral College is outdated and unfair, as it disregards the popular vote in some cases. For instance, in the 2016 election, Hillary Clinton received nearly 2.9 million more votes than Donald Trump, yet he won the presidency due to the Electoral College. This has led to calls for reform or even elimination of the Electoral College. On the other hand, supporters of the Electoral College argue that it maintains the balance between states and ensures that the interests of smaller states are not overshadowed by those of larger states. They also claim that the Electoral College prevents regional candidates from being elected, as they would have to garner a majority of votes across the country. In conclusion, the Electoral College has been a topic of controversy since its inception. While some argue it's outdated and unfair, others believe it preserves the balance between large and small states. Regardless, the Electoral College continues to play a significant role in the U.S. Presidential election process, with the 2016 election highlighting its potential flaws and the ongoing debate about its effectiveness.

The Facial Action Coding System (FACS) is a way to analyze and classify facial expressions. Developed by Dr. Paul Ekman and Dr. Wallace Friesen, it provides a standardized method for studying and identifying the movements and muscle actions involved in various human emotions. FACS breaks down facial expressions into a comprehensive set of action units (AUs). AUs are distinct components that, when combined, form the overall expression. Each AU represents a specific muscle action or movement, such as raising the eyebrows, wrinkling the nose, or compressing the lips. By analyzing these AUs, scientists can better understand the complexities of human emotions, as well as the universal nature of certain facial expressions. This system has been extensively researched and applied in various fields, including psychology, neuroscience, and computer science. One of the most significant applications of FACS is the development of emotion recognition technology. By analyzing facial expressions using AUs, researchers can create algorithms that can accurately identify and categorize emotions in real-time. This technology is already being utilized in various industries, such as advertising, entertainment, and healthcare, to improve the overall user experience and understanding of human emotions. In summary, the FACS is a valuable tool for studying and classifying facial expressions. It allows researchers to deconstruct complex emotions into simple AUs, providing a comprehensive understanding of human emotions and their universal nature. Additionally, this system has led to the development of emotion recognition technology with various real-life applications.

We examine how well people learn when information is noisily relayed from person to person; and we study how communication platforms can improve learning without censoring or fact-checking messages. We analyze learning as a function of social network depth (how many times information is relayed) and breadth (the number of relay chains accessed). Noise builds up as depth increases, so learning requires greater breadth. In the presence of mutations (deliberate or random) and transmission failures of messages, we characterize sharp thresholds for breadths above which receivers learn fully and below which they learn nothing. When there is uncertainty about mutation rates, optimizing learning requires either capping depth, or if that is not possible, limiting breadth by capping the number of people to whom someone can forward a message. Limiting breadth cuts the number of messages received but also decreases the fraction originating further from the receiver, and so can increase the signal to noise ratio. Finally, we extend our model to study learning from message survival: e.g., people are more likely to pass messages with one conclusion than another. We find that as depth grows, all learning comes from either the total number of messages received or from the content of received messages, but the learner does not need to pay attention to both. Sure! DNA is like a set of instructions for your body. It's made up of small units called nucleotides, which are arranged in a specific order that spells out the instructions.

Inside each of your cells, there are tiny machines called ribosomes that read the instructions in your DNA. They do this by using a special chemical called RNA, which copies the instructions from the DNA and carries them to the ribosomes.

The ribosomes then use the instructions from the RNA to make proteins, which are special molecules that do all sorts of important jobs in your body. For example, proteins can help build new cells, fight off infections, and even carry messages from one part of your body to another.

So, to sum it up: your cells use special machines called ribosomes to read the instructions in your DNA and make proteins based on those instructions. The proteins do all sorts of important things in your body to keep you healthy and working properly.

Exploring Venus Venus, the second planet from the sun, is an incredible place in our solar system. It is sometimes referred to as Earth's "twin," due to their similar size and composition; however, there are many differences between these two planets. Venus has an extremely thick atmosphere, composed mainly of carbon dioxide, and its surface experiences extreme temperatures, ranging from 864 degrees Fahrenheit (462 degrees Celsius) during the day, to -292 degrees Fahrenheit (-180 degrees Celsius) at night, which are the hottest and coldest temperatures experienced in our solar system. Scientists have been fascinated by Venus for years, and there have been numerous explorations of this mysterious planet. The Soviet Union's Venera 7 mission in 1970 was the first spacecraft to successfully land on another planet's surface and send data back to Earth. This mission, as well as the following Venera missions, provided crucial information about Venus's atmosphere, weather, and geology. One interesting aspect of Venus is its dense atmosphere, which makes studying its surface extremely challenging. The only way to directly observe the surface is through spacecraft equipped with specialized technology. The United States' Magellan mission in 1990 utilized radar to map the surface, providing detailed images and data about the planet. Another exciting exploration of Venus was the ESA's Venus Express mission, which began in 2006 and lasted until 2014. This mission used advanced technology to study the atmosphere, clouds, and weather patterns on the planet. The data collected by Venus Express has contributed greatly to our understanding of Venus and its unique characteristics. In addition to these past missions, there have been discussions about future explorations of Venus. The NASA InSight mission, which launched in 2018, is expected to study the planet's internal structure, seismology, and geological processes. Additionally, the proposed European-Russian Venera-D (or Venera-D) mission aims to study the atmosphere, clouds, and weather patterns on Venus using advanced technology, including a lander capable of withstanding extreme temperatures and pressures. Exploring Venus is crucial for our knowledge of the solar system and our understanding of the formation and evolution of planets. As we continue to learn more about this fascinating world, we may unlock secrets about our own planet Earth, as well as the universe around us.

Driverless cars have become a topic of immense interest in recent years. As technology continues to advance, the possibility of autonomous vehicles becoming a reality is becoming increasingly likely. In this essay, we will explore the benefits and drawbacks of driverless cars, and consider the impact they could have on our society. On the one hand, driverless cars could have a profoundly positive impact on our traffic patterns. With the ability to communicate with each other, vehicles could travel more efficiently, with fewer accidents and slower journeys. This could potentially reduce congestion, and decrease the overall time it takes for people to get around. Another benefit of driverless cars is the reduction in the number of accidents caused by human error. Many of the accidents on our roads are caused by mistakes made by drivers, such as speeding, running red lights, or drunk driving. With the use of advanced sensors and computer vision, autonomous vehicles could eliminate these human errors, significantly reducing the number of accidents on our roads. Additionally, driverless cars could offer greater accessibility to vehicles for those who are unable to drive, such as the elderly or people with disabilities. This could enable these individuals to travel more independently, and improve their overall quality of life. Despite these benefits, there are also potential drawbacks to driverless cars. One concern is the cost of the technology required to make these cars autonomous. At present, the technology is expensive, and it may be many years before the cost of implementing driverless cars nationwide becomes feasible. Another concern is the impact on jobs, as many jobs that are currently performed by human drivers, such as taxi drivers or delivery drivers, could become obsolete in the face of autonomous vehicles. This could lead to widespread unemployment, and a significant economic impact. In conclusion, driverless cars are an exciting prospect that holds the potential for significant societal benefits. However, it is important that the potential drawbacks are also seriously considered, and addressed in advance. As a society, we must be proactive in planning for the widespread adoption of autonomous vehicles, and take steps to mitigate any negative impact.

A standard adult football match consists of two periods of 45 minutes each, known as halves. Each half runs continuously, meaning that the clock is not stopped when the ball is out of play. There is usually a 15-minute half-time break between halves. The end of the match is known as full-time. The referee is the official timekeeper for the match, and may make an allowance for time lost through substitutions, injured players requiring attention, or other stoppages. This added time is called additional time in FIFA documents, but is most commonly referred to as stoppage time or injury time, while loss time can also be used as a synonym. The duration of stoppage time is at the sole discretion of the referee. The referee alone signals the end of the match. In matches where a fourth official is appointed, toward the end of the half the referee signals how many minutes of stoppage time he intends to add. The fourth official then informs the players and spectators by holding up a board showing this number. The signalled stoppage time may be further extended by the referee. Added time was introduced because of an incident which happened in 1891 during a match between Stoke and Aston Villa. Trailing 1-0 and with just two minutes remaining, Stoke were awarded a penalty. Villa's goalkeeper kicked the ball out of the ground, and by the time the ball had been recovered, the 90 minutes had elapsed and the game was over. The same law also states that the duration of either half is extended until the penalty kick to be taken or retaken is completed, thus no game shall end with a penalty to be taken.

Candidates have incentives to build broader coalitions across many states rather than just focusing campaigns on population centers. This helps ensure that voters from rural areas and smaller states still feel represented in national elections. A strictly popular vote could result in candidates ignoring several regions of the country. On balance, maintaining the Electoral College upholds federalist principles of balanced representation in our large, diverse country. In conclusion, while the Electoral College is imperfect, on the whole it has served our democracy reasonably well for many years in achieving goals like broader geographic representation, respecting federalist principles, and avoiding extremes. By monitoring user behavior and interests, the app can curate a personalized feed tailored to each individual user. As a result, users consistently find new content they're interested in, which keeps them coming back for more. Second, TikTok also takes advantage of our natural tendency to be curious and explore new things. The "For You" page features an ever-changing selection of videos, which encourages users to keep scrolling and watching to see what's next. This helps keep the feed fresh and exciting, and it prevents users from getting bored or losing interest. Finally, the platform also taps into our need for social validation. Every time someone likes or comments on a video, the user feels seen and heard, which reinforces their desire to keep engaging with the app. TikTok's success is no accident; the platform was deliberately designed to be as addictive as possible. By understanding the psychology behind its popularity, we can better understand why it's so successful.

The sun was blazing hot in the sky and it seemed to be getting hotter by the minute. Less flippantly , it exists because resources are scarce . Money helps us decide how to allocate scarce resources . For example : there is a limited amount of beautiful , beachfront property on earth . How do we decide who should get to use that property ? Money provides us the answer - whoever is willing to pay the most for use of the property , gets to use it . It is important to note that money is just * one possible * system for allocating scarce resources . Money has some advantages , which I will get into . But there are other possibilities . For example , you could allocate scarce resources by decree , with a committee deciding who gets the beachfront property . Or , you could allocate scarce resources by whoever gets it first . Whoever first builds a house on the property gets it . The advantage to using money to allocate scarce resources is that money can generally only be made by being a productive member of society . And that means making life better for people , because if you did n't , they would n't give you their money ! That 's the theory , anyway , and plenty of people would disagree with it , but the fact is that it 's worked damn well for Western civilization so far , problems and all . Are there * better * ways to allocate resources than money ? Maybe ! Who knows ! Money is certainly very well tested . So if you want to do away with money , then you have to come up with an alternate system of allocating scarce resources . Because resources will * always * be scarce . Even if everyone on earth had all the food they wanted , and we somehow managed to make everyone an Xbox 360 and a nice car , beachfront property would still be in limited supply . As would Ferraris and 20 carat emeralds . All of these need to be allocated somehow . How do you propose to do that ?

The meaning and origin of many archaic festivals baffled even Rome's intellectual elite, but the more obscure they were, the greater the opportunity for reinvention and reinterpretation - a fact lost neither on Augustus in his program of religious reform, which often cloaked autocratic innovation, nor on his only rival as mythmaker of the era, Ovid. In his Fasti, a long-form poem covering Roman holidays from January to June, Ovid presents a unique look at Roman antiquarian lore, popular customs, and religious practice that is by turns imaginative, entertaining, high-minded, and scurrilous; not a priestly account, despite the speaker's pose as a vates or inspired poet-prophet, but a work of description, imagination and poetic etymology that reflects the broad humor and burlesque spirit of such venerable festivals as the Saturnalia, Consualia, and feast of Anna Perenna on the Ides of March, where Ovid treats the assassination of the newly deified Julius Caesar as utterly incidental to the festivities among the Roman people. But official calendars preserved from different times and places also show a flexibility in omitting or expanding events, indicating that there was no single static and authoritative calendar of required observances. In the later Empire under Christian rule, the new Christian festivals were incorporated into the existing framework of the Roman calendar, alongside at least some of the traditional festivals.

In recent years, the growing population and urbanization have led to an unprecedented surge in traffic congestion and housing problems in major cities worldwide. The idea of moving large companies, factories, and their employees to the countryside has been proposed as a potential solution to these issues. While this idea may seem like a viable option, there are several reasons to believe that it would not be the most effective solution. Firstly, relocating big companies and factories to the countryside would not necessarily alleviate the traffic problem in major cities. Traffic congestion is primarily caused by the influx of people commuting to and from work. Even if factories and corporations were to move to the countryside, employees would still need to travel to and from their new workplaces, which would likely result in increased traffic on rural roads. Secondly, the housing problem in major cities is often a result of limited available land and high demand for living spaces. By moving factories and companies to the countryside, this would not necessarily create more housing opportunities in the cities. In fact, it could exacerbate the problem by further reducing the demand for urban housing and causing a decline in property values. Moreover, there are economic implications to consider. Major cities are often hubs for innovation, growth, and economic development. By moving big companies and factories away from these urban centers, it could potentially stifle economic growth and development, as well as lead to job losses for those who are unable to relocate to the countryside or find employment elsewhere. Another concern is the potential negative environmental impacts of such a move. Relocating large industries to rural areas could lead to increased pollution and land degradation, as well as displacement of local communities who rely on the land for their livelihoods. In conclusion, while the idea of moving big companies, factories, and their employees to the countryside may seem like an attractive solution to traffic and housing problems in major cities, it is essential to consider the potential economic, social, and environmental consequences of such a move. Instead, a more sustainable and comprehensive approach that includes urban planning, transportation infrastructure development, and affordable housing policies should be considered to address these issues more effectively.

There has, however, been interest among railroad operators in returning to DC use at higher voltages than previously used. At the same voltage, DC often has less loss than AC, and for this reason high-voltage direct current is already used on some bulk power transmission lines. DC avoids the electromagnetic radiation inherent with AC, and on a railway this also reduces interference with signalling and communications and mitigates hypothetical EMF risks. DC also avoids the power factor problems of AC. Of particular interest to railroading is that DC can supply constant power with a single ungrounded wire. Constant power with AC requires three-phase transmission with at least two ungrounded wires. Another important consideration is that mains-frequency 3-phase AC must be carefully planned to avoid unbalanced phase loads. Parts of the system are supplied from different phases on the assumption that the total loads of the 3 phases will even out. At the phase break points between regions supplied from different phases, long insulated supply breaks are required to avoid them being shorted by rolling stock using more than one pantograph at a time. A few railroads have tried 3-phase but its substantial complexity has made single-phase standard practice despite the interruption in power flow that occurs twice every cycle. An experimental 6 kV DC railway was built in the Soviet Union.

In general, the saying "a little knowledge is a dangerous thing" suggests that having a small amount of information on a subject can lead to mistakes, misunderstandings, and even dangerous consequences. While it's essential to have some knowledge on a topic, it can be harmful if we rely solely on a limited amount of information without understanding the broader context. For example, let's consider a scenario where an individual with little knowledge about electrical wiring tries to install a new outlet without proper training. They may have read a few online tutorials or watched a video, but their limited knowledge may not be enough to ensure safe installation. As a result, they could potentially put themselves and others at risk of electrical shock or even a fire. Similarly, in the field of medicine, a person with a little knowledge may self-diagnose and self-medicate without fully understanding the potential risks and side effects of their actions. This could lead to worsening their health condition, incorrect treatments, or even addiction. Another example is when people rely on rumors, fake news, and misinformation as a basis for their opinions and beliefs. This limited knowledge can lead to biased, irrational, and sometimes harmful actions towards individuals or groups. In conclusion, a little knowledge can indeed be a dangerous thing if we don't acknowledge its limitations and seek to expand our understanding beyond the superficial level. It's essential to be open-minded, seek out reliable sources, and continually educate ourselves to avoid the potential dangers of having only limited knowledge.

When you're in a dark room, your rods are more active and your cones are less active, which is why it can be harder to see colors in the dark. Wi-Fi is basically just a two-way radio system. There's a few different ranges of frequencies that are allowed for personal use. If you have a large house, 2.4GHz (the "NetgearXX" network on your router) will reach out to the ends of your house better, and it's very likely that both networks will be fast enough that it doesn't matter which one you use. But if you live in a dense urban area, the 5GHz network (the -5G network) will have less interference from your neighbors (since it's less common and shorter range), so if your devices can see that network, it'll work better. Some older or cheaper devices may not support the 5GHz network at all, in which case it won't even show up in their list of networks.

Interrelation of Ramadan Fasting and Pregnancy Essay There is no doubt that Ramadan fasting among Muslim women has long-term effects on the well-being of unborn babies. The majority of studies done on this issue have only addressed the short-term outcomes of Ramadan fasting among pregnant Muslim women. For example, Arab and Nasrollahi (2001) conducted a cross-sectional study to determine the relationship between fetal birth weight and fasting during pregnancy (p.91). Although the findings of the study revealed a positive correlation between fetal birth weight and fasting during pregnancy, the outcomes were only based on the assessment of participants during Ramadan (Arab & Nasrollahi, 2001, p.91). In another cross-sectional study done by Kamyabi and Naderi (2004), participants were assessed to determine the effect of Ramadan fasting on amniotic fluid (p.45). However, this study only reported the short-term effects of Ramadan fasting on amniotic fluid (Kamyabi & Naderi, 2004, p.46). Fasting among pregnant women is likely to affect the normal growth and development of babies in later years. Therefore, the principal aim of this research is to investigate and analyze the long-term effects of Ramadan fasting among pregnant Muslim women on unborn babies. This research topic is important because it will create awareness among policymakers and prenatal caregivers. For example, this research topic will enable healthcare administrators in advising pregnant fasting women on appropriate measures to be taken to protect their unborn babies from the long-term effects of Ramadan fasting. Moreover, this research topic will be used as a knowledge base for future studies on the long-term effects of Ramadan fasting among pregnant Muslim women on unborn babies. References Arab, M and Nasrollahi, S. (2001). Interrelation of Ramadan Fasting and Birth Weight. Medical Journal of Islamic Academy of Sciences, 14, 91-95. Kamyabi, Z., and Naderi, T. (2004). Deductive vs. Inductive Reasoning in Everyday Life Report Deductive and inductive reasoning are both methods of reaching logically true conclusions used in scientific research as well as everyday life. Very often, they are confused. That is why a clear distinction between them should be made. As defined by Anderson (2015), deductive reasoning, or deduction, is relevant to the conclusion that surely follows the assumption (p. 239). That means that the one using deduction assumes that what is true of a certain group of objects is also true about every single object from this group, i.e., reaching a logical conclusion starts with a general statement based on which the conclusion about observations is made. In inductive reasoning, unlike deductive, the conclusion does not necessarily follow the assumptions (Anderson, 2015, p. 251), and using induction, the general statement is reached by using observations. That means that the conclusion is made after analyzing aspects of the problem, e.g., studying symptoms to make a diagnosis. The only problem with this method is that a particular set of observations does not always lead to the same general statement. Coming back to symptoms studied to make a diagnosis, the same set of symptoms may refer to different diseases. To see the difference between the two, it may be useful to draw an example. Let us assume that Mary and Max are married, and Mindy is Mary’s daughter. One might conclude that Max is Mindy’s father, and Max is older than Mary. As for “Max is Mindy’s father,” it is a correct deductive inference, but “Max is older than Mary” may not be true, so it is a good inductive inference, but it may not be a correct deductive inference. So, deductive and inductive reasoning are both useful in reaching logical conclusions, but sometimes it might be difficult to define which method should be used to reach a conclusion that is true. References Anderson, J. R. (2015). Cognitive psychology and its implications (8th ed.). New York, NY: Worth Publishers.

Furthermore, families often play a role in helping provide emotional support too—sometimes even more so than professional assistance!. . The electoral college, as a part of the United States' presidential election process, has been a topic of much discussion and debate. The main purpose of the electoral college is to serve as a mechanism for indirectly electing the President and Vice President of the United States. The system was created during the Constitutional Convention in 1787, as a compromise between electing the President by popular vote and having the legislators select the President. The electoral college system consists of a total of 538 electoral votes. These electoral votes are divided among the 50 states, with each state receiving a number of votes based on its representation in both the House of Representatives and the Senate. Additionally, there is one electoral vote per congressional district, and two additional votes for Washington D.C., for a total of 538 votes. When a citizen casts their vote for President during a general election, they are actually voting for a group of electors, known as electors, who will then cast votes in the Electoral College. Each state's electors are chosen in one of two ways: by popular vote or by state legislatures. The electoral college system is controversial for various reasons. One of the primary concerns is that it can lead to the candidate winning the popular vote but not the electoral college vote. This has happened several times in the history of the United States, including the 2016 election, which led many people to question the effectiveness of the electoral college system. Additionally, some argue that the electoral college system disproportionately favors smaller states, as each state receives two votes in the Electoral College regardless of population. Furthermore, the system can lead to the winner-takes-all situation in states, where the candidate with the most votes in a state wins all of the state's electoral votes, potentially causing the losing candidate to receive no electoral college votes at all. In conclusion, the electoral college system works in the sense that it serves its intended purpose of indirectly electing the President and Vice President of the United States. However, it also has various drawbacks that have led to debates about its effectiveness and potential reform.

Much of Brittonic-controlled Britain was conquered by the Roman Empire from AD 43. The first Anglo-Saxons arrived as Roman power waned in the 5th century and eventually dominated the bulk of what is now England. Viking invasions began in the 9th century, followed by more permanent settlements and political change - particularly in England. The subsequent Norman conquest of England in 1066 and the later Angevin partial conquest of Ireland from 1169 led to the imposition of a new Norman ruling elite across much of Britain and parts of Ireland. By the Late Middle Ages, Great Britain was separated into the Kingdoms of England and Scotland, while control in Ireland fluxed between Gaelic kingdoms, Hiberno-Norman lords and the English-dominated Lordship of Ireland, soon restricted only to The Pale. The 1603 Union of the Crowns, Acts of Union 1707 and Acts of Union 1800 attempted to consolidate Britain and Ireland into a single political unit, the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland, with the Isle of Man and the Channel Islands remaining as Crown Dependencies. The expansion of the British Empire and migrations following the Irish Famine and Highland Clearances resulted in the distribution of the islands' population and culture throughout the world and a rapid de-population of Ireland in the second half of the 19th century. Most of Ireland seceded from the United Kingdom after the Irish War of Independence and the subsequent Anglo-Irish Treaty , with six counties remaining in the UK as Northern Ireland.

In addition to Beatrice's edited copy, Lord Esher transcribed the volumes from 1832 to 1861 before Beatrice destroyed them. The Codex Justinianus (1:5:12) defines "everyone who is not devoted to the Catholic Church and to our Orthodox holy Faith" a heretic. The Church had always dealt harshly with strands of Christianity that it considered heretical, but before the 11th century these tended to centre around individual preachers or small localised sects, like Arianism, Pelagianism, Donatism, Marcionism and Montanism. The diffusion of the almost Manichaean sect of Paulicians westwards gave birth to the famous 11th and 12th century heresies of Western Europe. The first one was that of Bogomils in modern day Bosnia, a sort of sanctuary between Eastern and Western Christianity. By the 11th century, more organised groups such as the Patarini, the Dulcinians, the Waldensians and the Cathars were beginning to appear in the towns and cities of northern Italy, southern France and Flanders.
