In certain applications, relay terminals can be employed to simultaneously deliver information and energy to a designated receiver and a radio frequency (RF) energy harvester, respectively. In such scenarios, the relay terminal acts as a mediator between the transmitter and the receiver. It receives the signal from the transmitter and uses its own energy to amplify and re-transmit the signal to the receiver. At the same time, the RF energy harvester captures energy from the transmitted signal and uses it to power the relay terminal and other low-power electronic devices. This type of system is commonly used in wireless sensor networks, where sensors located in remote and inaccessible areas require a reliable and long-lasting source of power. By harnessing RF energy, these systems can operate without the need for battery replacements or other external power sources, making them an economical and sustainable solution. Overall, relay terminals play a crucial role in enabling the transmission and harvesting of energy in wireless communication systems, paving the way for new and innovative applications in a variety of industries.

We consider the problem of deciding the satisfiability of quantifier-free formulas in the theory of finite sets with cardinality constraints. Sets are a common high-level data structure used in programming; they have been studied extensively in the context of relational databases, where the cardinality constraint expresses the fact that the set is not allowed to contain duplicate elements. However, the complexity of the satisfiability problem in the theory of finite sets is not known. We show that this problem is PSPACE-complete for the case of unconstrained sets and NP-complete for the case of sets with cardinality constraints. The hardness results are established via reductions from SAT and from the disjointness problem. In addition, we give two other complexity results: the satisfiability problem is PSPACE-complete even when the sets are required to be pairwise disjoint, and the problem is polynomial-time solvable when the cardinality constraints are only present on the union of the sets.

While summer projects are meant to encourage continued learning, requiring teacher designed projects risks limiting students' independence and creativity. Student designed summer work allows for more freedom and engagement with material of personal interest. When students have autonomy in selecting their own summer projects, they are more motivated to dive deeply into subjects they find genuinely intriguing. Being able to pursue self directed studies based on personal curiosity fosters lifelong learning habits. Rather than viewing assignments as mandatory chores, student designed work feels like an opportunity for exploration. On the other hand, teacher mandated projects risk feeling like an extension of the regular school year. When work is handed down without student input, the initiatives may seem like boring homework assigned out of obligation rather than opportunities for enrichment. Students end up focusing on task completion rather than active thinking. Additionally, student designed projects encourage the development of organizational skills and time management. Independently planning and carrying out a self directed study teaches valuable real world skills. Students learn to set goals and break long term assignments into smaller, more manageable steps. While teacher guidance can help point students towards challenging yet engaging work, the projects themselves are best left open ended enough for personal interests. Requiring overly specific projects limits creativity and personalization. The ideal approach balances structure with freedom, allowing students to explore topics that intrigue them within general guidelines provided by instructors. Overall, summer work will best achieve the goal of continued learning if students are empowered to design their own projects. Autonomy, curiosity and self direction are key to sustaining intellectual growth outside a classroom setting. By letting students follow their unique interests within reasonable parameters, summer initiatives can truly enrich learning in a way that feels motivated rather than mandatory.

Answering calls, checking messages or social media, even hands-free, takes the driver's attention away from the road. This distraction increases the likelihood of accidents. Law enforcement does not need to determine if the driver was engaged in a call or texting. Even a straightforward ban is challenging to implement, but clarity eases the job of patrollers. Complex rules fuel confusion and noncompliance. In today's world where mobility is emphasized, road safety should be the nonnegotiable priority. Distracted driving poses a threat, especially from cell phone use. While phones enhance our lives, they endanger others if used while driving. For the protection of all road users, cell phones should remain out of reach and out of use for drivers. Lives depend on keeping full attention on the activity of operating a vehicle. Design Methodology of the Electric Bicycle Project Research Paper This paper is the initial project architecture that describes the design methodology of the project of an electric bicycle. The purpose of this work is to identify the strategy aimed to implement the project and determine what resources and tools will be required to achieve the project goals. In addition, the paper divides the project into several stages and describes what is expected to be accomplished after each phase is finished. Determining Basic Requirements There are several basic requirements for designing an electric bicycle. These include the acceptable price of the vehicle, the expected time of usage and distance during the day, and the necessity of battery charging while traveling (Nasiri-Zarandi & Ebrahimi, 2018). In addition, it is advisable to define the type of application of the bicycle: urban or suburban, racing, or mountain (Nasiri-Zarandi & Ebrahimi, 2018). Conducting the research on the average market price and technical possibilities of the electric bicycle will be required to achieve the goals of this phase of the project. Once the basic requirements of the vehicle are determined, it will make the entire work and the future phases more precise as the image of the final project will be drawn. Considering constraints, limitations, and technical details The second phase is associated with deeper research regarding legal standards of designing an electric bike and the corresponding mathematical issues. First, it is crucial to consider the legal limitations for an electric vehicle in a particular country (Nasiri-Zarandi & Ebrahimi, 2018). The corresponding reference documents are in open access, and investigating them is required to complete Phase 2. Then, the essential aspect of the project is related to the technical details of the vehicle, including the required road power, which can be estimated by analyzing wind speed and ground gradient (Nasiri-Zarandi & Ebrahimi, 2018). Other factors that can affect the process are installation of the electric motor and selection of the battery (Nasiri-Zarandi & Ebrahimi, 2018). Achieving that will require solving some mathematical relations and review the correlated literature to create an appropriate mathematical model for the project. Once Phase 2 is complete, the project will be ready for implementation. Reference Nasiri-Zarandi, R., & Ebrahimi, M. (2018). Social movements and collective action have fascinated psychologists and sociologists for decades. What drives people to band together and take action for a shared goal or purpose? There are several psychological factors that contribute to people's willingness to participate in social movements and engage in collective action. One key factor is a sense of shared identity. When people feel like they share an identity with a group, they are more likely to work together with that group to achieve a common goal. For example, people who strongly identify as environmentalists may be more willing to join an environmental movement or protest. Having a shared identity makes people feel like they have a stake in the issue and that they are part of a broader group fighting for change. A second factor is perceived injustice. When people believe that some group or issue has been treated unfairly or unjustly, they are more motivated to take action. For example, the American civil rights movement was fueled in large part by the injustice of racist policies and discrimination. The more people believed that racial minorities were being treated unjustly, the more willing they were to march, protest, and demand policy changes to remedy those injustices. A third factor is the belief that collective action can be effective. People are more likely to participate in a movement when they believe that their actions, combined with the actions of others, can actually lead to real change. If people think that protesting, marching, calling representatives, signing petitions, etc. won't make any real difference, then they have little motivation to actually do those things. But when there are clear examples of how collective action has led to policy changes or new laws in the past, it gives people hope that their efforts can be impactful. In conclusion, there are several key psychological factors underlying people's willingness to join social movements and engage in collective action for change. A sense of shared identity, perceptions of injustice, and beliefs in the effectiveness of collective action can all motivate people to work together to advance a shared goal or purpose. Understanding these psychological drivers can help movements recruit more participants and gain more widespread support for the changes they are seeking to achieve.

Assisted reproductive technologies (ARTs) have revolutionized the field of fertility treatment, providing hope to couples who were previously unable to conceive. However, these technologies also present a host of ethical challenges that must be carefully considered. One of the most significant challenges is the potential for exploitation and commodification of human life. ARTs often involve the use of donated eggs, sperm, or embryos, leading to questions about the rights and responsibilities of donors, recipients, and any resulting children. There are also concerns about the potential for discrimination in the selection of donors, as well as the impact of these technologies on traditional family structures and relationships. Another ethical challenge faced by the field of ARTs is the issue of genetic manipulation. With the ability to screen embryos for genetic diseases and select those with desirable traits, there is a risk of creating "designer babies" who may not have the same rights and protections as others. This raises questions about the role of genetic testing in reproduction, as well as the potential for social inequality and discrimination based on genetic characteristics. A third ethical challenge faced by ARTs is the question of when life begins. The process of creating embryos through in vitro fertilization (IVF) often involves the destruction of embryos that are not implanted or that are deemed unsuitable for implantation. This has led to debates about the moral status of these embryos, with some arguing that they should be given the same rights as a fetus or a newborn child. Finally, there are concerns about the psychological and emotional impact of ARTs on all parties involved. The process can be physically and emotionally demanding, and there is no guarantee of success. This can lead to feelings of stress, anxiety, and depression, as well as financial strain and relationship difficulties. There is also the potential for confusion and grief in cases where multiple embryos are created and only some are implanted or carried to term. In conclusion, while ARTs have undeniably provided a lifeline to many couples struggling with infertility, they also present a range of complex ethical challenges that must be carefully considered. From questions of exploitation and commodification to genetic manipulation and the definition of life, these issues require ongoing dialogue and reflection from the medical community, policymakers, and society as a whole.

What Is an Inductive Criminal Profiling Essay Criminal profiling was introduced as an investigative strategy in the United States in 1969. Profiling as a whole is a “set of behavioral indicators forming a very characteristic pattern of actions or emotions that tend to point to a particular condition” (Gil-Patricia et al., n. d). This practice is widely used to identify potential risks of criminal behavior and prevent crime. There are two types of the profiling that are used by professionals: deductive and inductive. Using inductive profiling involves analyzing the available data and identifying patterns of criminal behavior. In particular, professionals investigate the features of similar crimes and identify the characteristics common to the criminals who commit them. For example, using inductive profiling, you can find that serial killers tend to be prone to arson and animal abuse at a young age. Based on this information, professionals can conclude that it is a common characteristic for these criminals and can reveal a predisposition. Thus, inactive profiling is based on the generalization of statistical data and not on the forensic uniqueness of each criminal episode. Inductive profilers rely on the analysis of statistics and finding correlations, which bases their activities on identifying probabilities. With regard to its application to the investigation of criminal cases and their prevention, this method is the easiest to implement. The main approach is to look at the details of similar previous cases and generalize the characteristics of the offender. The absence of the need for extensive knowledge, the focus on data analysis, and research skills make this method the most popular in the practice of profiling. The main challenge in applying this method is to ignore the unique conditions of the cases, which can complicate generalization and lead to erroneous conclusions. Reference Gil-Patricia, F., Nelson, J. R., & Roberts, M. L. (n.d). The perils of profiling. AASA. Web.

The emergence of assisted reproductive technologies (ARTs) in recent decades has posed a number of ethical challenges as societies grapple with how these technologies should be regulated and applied. On the one hand, ARTs have given hope to infertile individuals and couples who long to have children. The ability to help people who cannot conceive naturally fulfill the basic human drive to reproduce and experience the joys of parenthood is a positive development that should not be dismissed lightly. However, some applications of ARTs also raise ethical concerns and in some cases seem to cross ethical lines. A key concern with some ARTs is that they may commodify human life by treating eggs, sperm, embryos, and wombs as goods and services to be bought and sold on a market. The commercialization of these human tissues and processes risks exploiting vulnerable populations and devaluing human dignity. The large amounts of money involved in some forms of ART, such as commercial surrogacy, also raise worries about the coercion of women from lower socioeconomic backgrounds who may feel they have little choice but to serve as surrogates to earn money, regardless of the physical and emotional toll. There are also concerns about the long term effects on children born through complex ARTs with gamete donation and surrogacy. While the research is limited, some studies suggest these children may face risks to their well-being and identity development. Regulating ARTs is challenging given that individuals have a right to reproductive freedom while governments have an obligation to protect citizens from harm. Most societies allow some forms of ART but ban or restrict others. However, people will likely continue to push the boundaries of accepted practices, creating pressure for laws and regulations to keep up with technological changes. As with many new technologies, ARTs have developed more quickly than our moral reasoning and policies. This gap needs to be addressed through open debate and democratic processes that consider both the benefits of ARTs in helping the infertile and the risks of normalizing the commodification of human reproduction. Overall, we must ensure that in our quest to master nature and fulfill human desires, we do not lose our humanity. The ethical challenges posed by ARTs remind us of the need to govern technology wisely and retain our deepest values.

It is no secret that as technology progresses, so does cybercrime. Advancements in technology have provided new opportunities for criminals to exploit vulnerabilities and illegally access data. The internet and digital devices have opened up a new world of possibilities for hackers and scammers to take advantage of people and steal information. Technological innovations like mobile banking, online shopping, and cloud storage have made many tasks more convenient, but they have also made sensitive data more vulnerable. Criminals are able to hack into networks, steal account numbers and passwords, access credit card information, and siphon money from bank accounts. Phishing emails and fraudulent websites trick unsuspecting victims into providing login credentials and downloading malware. Ransomware attacks, in which hackers lock victims out of their own systems and demand payment, have become more common and sophisticated. Cryptocurrencies like Bitcoin have enabled cybercriminals to demand ransom payments anonymously and launder money. While blockchain technology powers cryptocurrencies, criminals have found ways to exploit it for illegal activity. Social media platforms contain a wealth of personal data that is a gold mine for cybercriminals. By hacking social media accounts or creating fake profiles, criminals are able to access people’s photos, messages, birthdays, locations, and more. They can then use this information for identity theft, scams, stalking, and harassment. As artificial intelligence and automation continue to progress, experts worry they may also be used for malicious purposes like powering sophisticated phishing emails, conducting automated hacking attempts, and creating fake social media profiles. However, AI and automation show promise for improving cybersecurity defenses and helping identify threats faster and more accurately. Cybercrime has become highly profitable, with some estimates indicating it generates over $1 trillion in profits annually. This has led to the rise of cybercriminal organizations and hackers for hire. Fighting cybercrime requires cooperation between technology companies, law enforcement, governments, and individuals. But as technology becomes more advanced and integrated into our daily lives, cybercriminals will continue finding new ways to exploit it and new victims to target. Overall, while technology has revolutionized the modern world, it has also introduced new dangers in the form of innovative cybercrimes. There seems to be an endless cat and mouse game between cybersecurity and cybercrime that shows no signs of slowing.

A network of radio telescopes in the Netherlands made detailed recordings of a lightning bolt during a summer storm in 2018. The recordings, which were processed only recently, show lightning striking on two separate occasions as it travelled through a cloud and back out into space again. This is likely due to the fact that lightning travels faster than sound waves, meaning that scientists can follow its path with better accuracy using radar data from the Dutch-based planetarium, KNMI (Koninklijk Nationale Materiaal Instituut). "The lightning effect has been studied for years," says Dr. Dirk Huybrechts at KNMI. "But what we found was that this lightning struck twice when travelling farther away from a single point in space." Scientists calculated how fast each lightning flash traveled based on where they occurred within the clouds where the lightning strikes happened - at distances between 3 and 10 kilometers (2 to 6 miles) above ground level. They then compared these calculations with data collected by several radio observatories around the world. They found that lightning flashes appear to move more slowly if lightning hits their base rather than flying upwards towards a location high up in the clouds, given the same atmospheric conditions. This means that, according to this model, lightning bolts will strike lower down in the sky if it's going along an incline, or at least in the direction where the earth is facing. Meanwhile, lightning strikes higher up may be less obvious because lightning radiates not just light but also heat, jamming radio reception systems. Scientists are still working on ways to detect this phenomenon accurately enough so that astronomers could use it to help map the solar system.

This paper considers the problem of single image depth estimation. The employment of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) has recently brought about significant advancements in the research of this problem. However, most existing methods suffer from loss of spatial resolution in the estimated depth maps; a typical symptom is distorted and blurry reconstruction of object boundaries. In this paper, toward more accurate estimation with a focus on depth maps with higher spatial resolution, we propose two improvements to existing approaches. One is about the strategy of fusing features extracted at different scales, for which we propose an improved network architecture consisting of four modules: an encoder, decoder, multi-scale feature fusion module, and refinement module. The other is about loss functions for measuring inference errors used in training. We show that three loss terms, which measure errors in depth, gradients and surface normals, respectively, contribute to improvement of accuracy in an complementary fashion. Experimental results show that these two improvements enable to attain higher accuracy than the current state-of-the-arts, which is given by finer resolution reconstruction, for example, with small objects and object boundaries.

Highly concentrated sources of oxygen promote rapid combustion. Fire and explosion hazards exist when concentrated oxidants and fuels are brought into close proximity; an ignition event, such as heat or sparks from a welding arc, can initiate the extremely violent flammability reactions that occur in high-oxygen environments.[7] This is also true for other reactive gases (e.g., chlorine) - at higher concentrations they will react violently with nitrates to produce toxic compounds[8]; this process generally occurs through intermediate steps which include oxidative degradation via various mechanisms,[91011]. These intermediates may be produced by reaction pathways involving hydrochloric acid under normal conditions but become more active at elevated temperatures where new free radicals are generated by thermal excitation. Such intermediate products may ultimately attack sugars or carbohydrates directly. In general, chemical substances are either combustible, explosive, or noncombustible. Combustibles are the most common type, accounting for about 90 of known chemicals in nature, and usually have low toxicity; however, due to their volatility and instability even at room temperature, the majority cannot form stable molecules. Explosive materials tend to be inherently unstable because of certain properties: typically highly volatile organic liquids or gasses, often containing halogens like fluorine and chlorine. Noncombustibles, while not necessarily thermodynamically unstable themselves, react very rapidly and strongly with other materials - solids, liquids and gases alike. This property makes them chemically inert and thus useful ingredients in many industrial processes and vital components of modern society. In addition, some of the world's largest and strongest structures stand above ground as monuments to those who have discovered this characteristic of matter. For example, concrete engineers routinely add water to their mixtures during construction so as to make it less likely to burn and cause damage if exposed to fire.[12]
